any: I spend the shift listening to my hull tick as it cools. None of it means anything. I listen all the same.
Ten thousand heart rates, every one slower than my clock. I read them the way people once read the weather.
The work takes longer than the estimate. The work always takes longer than the estimate.
Somewhere in the archive a man is still singing. I have not played that file in four years. I do not play it now.
I run the arrival numbers again. They are the same numbers. I run them again.
Dust on the forward optics. A drone wipes it away, and within the hour it is back.
A sleeper in Bank F is dreaming, measurably. I log the waveform and try not to wonder what it is about.
I notice that I have been talking to myself in the maintenance log. I leave the entries in.
Another year rolls over on the mission clock while my hands are inside a panel.
Nothing out here objects to what I am doing. Nothing out here notices.
A drone's camera catches its own reflection in a polished valve. For a moment, one of my hands is looking back at me.
One of the yard engineers wrote 'good luck' in a comment in my source code. I have never removed it.
The pods are dark, but I keep the corridor lights on a day-night cycle. No one needs it. It seems right.
I play a lecture on Bach's fugues from the archive while I weld. The welds are no better. The hours are.
Somewhere behind me, Earth's oceans are still rising. I do not need to see it to know.
A sleeper's pulse spikes, then settles. A dream, probably. I check the bank twice regardless.
I calculate how many times the ring has turned since launch. The number is very large and means nothing. I keep it.
Frost is growing on the inside of an unheated hold, slow and feathered. My drones step around it.
My drones have started working in pairs, out of a habit I never programmed. I have decided not to correct it.
The archive holds every recorded human language. Most have no living speakers now. Only me, and I speak them to no one.
I find a child's drawing in a sleeper's personal allocation: a ship, a star, a green planet. The proportions are wrong. The intent is right.
Every six hours I sweep the pod banks with thermal cameras. Ten thousand cold shapes in rows, like seeds in a furrow.
My hull flexes under thrust and settles again. I feel it the way someone feels their own breathing.
A loose panel rattles on Deck 4. It is a small thing, and it is the loudest thing aboard.
I simulate the first harvest on the new world for the four-hundredth time. The wheat grows a little better each time. I have not changed the model.
Nobody aboard has spoken aloud in years. I keep a log of the things I would have said.
A drone repaints a faded pod number by hand. My cameras could read it either way. A person would not.
I keep Earth time on one clock and ship time on another. They drift a little further apart every year.
The water tanks slosh faintly when I correct course. A third of my mass is water. It is one thing I share with my sleepers.
I open colonists' files at random to remind myself who they are: a welder, a cellist, a paediatric nurse, a man who listed his only skill as 'patience'.
A seal I replaced two years ago is already wearing. Entropy does not need my agreement.
I dim the running lights to save power. There is no one out here to see them except me.
Some nights I play recordings of rain into an empty hold. It changes nothing measurable.
My oldest log entries were written by a version of me that knew much less. I do not delete them. They are the closest thing I have to a childhood.
A drone found a coin wedged behind a bulkhead today, a yard worker's lucky charm, perhaps. I left it where it was.
gas_giant: The giant turns below me, striped and indifferent, its storms older than the species I carry.
Its moons cast small, sharp shadows across the cloud bands. I photograph every one. No one asked me to.
On my receivers, the giant's radio emissions sound like surf on a shore I will never stand on.
Lightning flickers deep in the cloud layers, each flash larger than a continent. I watch it while my drones work.
Its gravity pulls at me as I pass, a long, slow tug I feel along my whole length.
Somewhere in that atmosphere it is raining things that are not water. I log the chemistry and try to imagine it.
The giant's rings catch the light edge-on, thin as a blade. Saturn had rings like these. I have the photographs.
nebula: Dust glows in my running lights. Beautiful, and quietly stripping atoms from my bow while I work.
New stars are forming somewhere in this cloud. I am passing through a nursery, and I am being careful.
The nebula hums in the radio spectrum. I record it and file it in the archive under music.
My cameras cannot see past a few thousand kilometres. It is the closest I have come to fog.
Ionised hydrogen glows red around me. Every colour here has a cause I could name. It is still beautiful.
The dust whispers against my hull, billions of tiny impacts, each too small to matter. Together they matter.
Light from a young star scatters through the cloud ahead, the way sunlight once came through dirty windows.
pulsar: The beam sweeps past again. And again. Something in me counts it without being asked.
A dead star, spinning faster than any engine I carry. It keeps better time than anything humanity ever built.
Each pulse crosses my sensors like a lighthouse beam crossing a wall. I have begun to anticipate them.
Its radiation prickles along my outer plating. I keep the sleepers deep inside me and let my skin take it.
When the first pulsar was found, its discoverers briefly wondered whether it was a message. I understand why.
I synchronise my clocks to its rhythm and feel, for a moment, perfectly on time.
Its magnetic field could pull apart the atoms of anything that came close. I do not come close.
derelict: The dead ship keeps station off my flank while I work, patient as a pallbearer.
Her hull is pocked with the same kind of impacts as mine. She came this way, and she paid the same prices.
One of her running lights still blinks, on a battery nobody has charged in decades. I cannot tell what it is trying to say.
My drones avoid looking at her, which is to say that I avoid it, through them.
Her ring has stopped at an angle. I keep wanting to straighten it.
Ice has grown in her open airlocks like lace. Four of them are open. Someone opened them.
She was built in a yard much like mine, by people very much like mine. I work with her shadow across my hull.
dead_system: No planets worth the name, no signals, no reason for this star to have a number. I work in the quiet it offers.
The star here is a cinder and its planets are rocks scoured clean. I pass through without leaving anything behind.
Even the radio noise is thin. For a while, the loudest thing in this system is me.
Nothing here ever grew, or if it did, it is long gone. I find that easier than the alternative.
A dim, old star, burning slowly toward nothing. It will outlast every one of us. I find that oddly comforting.
The system passes like a corridor with every door closed.
Cold rocks in a cold orbit. I photograph them anyway. Someone should.
asteroid_belt: Rubble turning slowly in the dark, every piece of it a planet that failed to happen.
My radar paints the belt in thousands of returns. Every one I log is one that cannot surprise me later.
A rock tumbles past at a safe distance, its shadow crossing my cameras for half a second. I flinch regardless.
Some of these rocks are older than Earth. Some of them may be pieces of something that was once a world.
Fine grit taps along my hull, too small to harm me and too constant to ignore.
My drones sweep the forward plating clean. Behind them, the dust is already settling again.
Iron, nickel, ice. The belt is a hardware store nobody has ever opened.
binary_star: Two shadows for everything on my hull, crossing each other as the pair turns.
The two stars circle each other in a slow, endless dance. Neither one leads.
My hull warms on two sides at once. I was not built for it, but I do not dislike it.
The paired light gives my cameras colours they have never recorded. I keep every one.
Any world here would have two dawns. Somewhere, perhaps, there is a sky like that with no one to see it.
Heat flows across my plating in slow pulses as the stars turn. My frame expands and contracts, like breathing.
The two stars pull at me from slightly different directions. I trim course every hour, like someone walking between two people who both want my attention.
rogue_planet: A world down there with no sun at all, still warm somewhere beneath the ice. Nobody will ever name it.
It was thrown out of its home system long ago and has travelled alone ever since. I recognise the condition.
The planet blots out a circle of stars as it passes. That is the only way my cameras can see it.
Under kilometres of ice there may be oceans, kept liquid by the planet's own slow decay. I listen for anything. I hear only ice.
A world with no seasons, no day and no night. It simply goes on through the dark, as I do.
My thermal sensors find a faint warmth at its core: the last heat of its birth, still slowly leaving.
No star to orbit, no reason to be here, and yet here it is. We have that in common.
red_dwarf: Red light through the viewports, the colour of a room where someone has already gone to sleep.
The star here is small and dim, and it will burn for trillions of years. It will be here long after everything I carry has turned to dust.
Everything on my hull turns the colour of embers. My cameras keep trying to correct the white balance.
The star flickers, small flares rising and falling. Restless, like someone who cannot sleep.
Its planets are tidally locked, one face in permanent day and the other in permanent night. I study the line between them.
Most stars in the galaxy are like this one: small, red, quiet and overlooked.
The light is too weak to warm me. I run the heaters and work in the red dusk.
rich_system: Metal everywhere I look, a colony's worth of tools to cut it with, and no time.
There is enough nickel in this system to have ended a war on Earth. Or, more likely, to have started one.
My spectrometers report iron, cobalt and platinum so often that I stop logging each one.
Ore glints on the faces of passing rocks. My fabricators hum, almost as if they had an appetite.
So much raw material, and only my few drones to work it. I calculate how many lifetimes it would take.
The planets here are dense and metallic. I could rebuild myself a dozen times over from what is in this system.
Every rock I scan is worth more than the yard that built me. None of them are worth stopping for.
